exercise.title: Why does integration by parts reverse the product rule?

statement.p: The product rule says d(uv)=u\,dv+v\,du. Rearranging and integrating produces \int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du. In your own words, why does this trade one integral for another rather than making an integral disappear for free, and when is the trade a good one?

hint.p: The formula helps only when the new integral is simpler than the old one. You are moving a derivative from one factor onto the other.

subsection.title: Choosing u and dv
subsection.p: requires a choice. We must decide which part of the integrand to call u, and which part to call dv.
The choice is not cosmetic. A good choice makes the remaining integral simpler. A poor choice makes it harder.

note.p: A good choice usually makes du simpler than u, while keeping v manageable.

exercise.title: What makes one choice of u and dv better than another?

statement.p: For \int x e^x\,dx, taking u=x simplifies the remaining integral, while taking u=e^x makes it worse. In your own words, why is the choice not cosmetic, and what should you want to happen to u when it is differentiated?

hint.p: Differentiate the factor that becomes simpler, and integrate the factor that stays manageable. A poor choice raises the power or complicates the remaining integral.

exercise.title: Why is one use of parts sometimes not enough?

statement.p: A power such as x^2 may need to be reduced one degree at a time, and some integrals cycle back to the original. In your own words, why can repeating the method, or naming the original integral and solving for it, still be reversing the product rule rather than starting over?

hint.p: Each pass peels one derivative off a factor. If the original integral returns, it has become an algebraic unknown that can be moved to the other side.

subsection.title: Definite integrals and boundary terms
subsection.p: For definite integrals, integration by parts has the same idea, but the product term is evaluated at the endpoints.

In an indefinite integral, this term appears as uv. In a definite integral, it becomes an endpoint contribution.

exercise.title: What is the boundary term in a definite integral?

statement.p: For definite integrals, integration by parts evaluates uv at the endpoints: \bigl[uv\bigr]_a^b. In your own words, why does that term come from the Fundamental Theorem, and why does it replace the standalone product uv that appears in the indefinite formula?

hint.p: Accumulating d(uv) from a to b is net change of the product. In an indefinite integral that net change has not yet been evaluated.

statement.p: No +C appears in a definite integral. The endpoint evaluation produces a number.
